stages.title: How Google Search Finds a Page
stages.description: Search is crawl, then index, then serving. Most pages are found by following links. Paying someone does not buy a higher rank.
learningObjectives: Name the three stages a page has to pass through
Explain how Google discovers a URL
Separate crawling from indexing and from ranking
State that payment does not buy a crawl or a rank

explainBack.question: A friend says they will pay to get a new page crawled more often and ranked higher. Explain what actually has to happen before that page can appear, and why the payment does not do that.
rubric: Google Search crawls pages with automated programs, indexes what it understands, then serves results for a query
There is no central registry of every page; URLs are discovered from links already crawled, from pages already visited, or from a sitemap
Googlebot does not crawl every URL it finds, and indexing is not guaranteed even after a page is processed
Google does not accept payment to crawl a site more often or to rank it higher
A page can be indexed and still not show for a query if the content is irrelevant or low quality

resources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
resources.description: Google's own account of crawling, indexing, and serving, including what is not guaranteed.
keyPoints: Search works in three stages: crawling, indexing, and serving search results, and not every page makes it through each stage
There is no central registry of web pages; Google discovers URLs from pages it already visited, from links on known pages, and from sitemaps
During a crawl Google renders the page and runs JavaScript with a recent version of Chrome, because otherwise it may not see the content
Indexing stores information about the chosen canonical page; indexing is not guaranteed
Google does not accept payment to crawl a site more frequently or to rank it higher, and ranking uses hundreds of factors including location, language, and device

resources.title: Introducing How Search Works
resources.description: The opening episode of Google's How Search Works series: crawling, indexing, and serving.
keyPoints: The series walks through crawling, indexing, and serving as the three stages of Search
Crawling is how Google discovers URLs and explores the web
Indexing is how Google understands what a page is about and stores that so it can be searched
Serving is how Google returns and ranks results for a query

resources.title: How Google Search indexes pages
resources.description: What happens after a page is crawled: reading the content and deciding whether to keep it in the index.
keyPoints: Indexing starts after the page has been crawled and rendered
Google processes the text, key content tags, attributes, images, and video, and calculates signals
Those signals help decide whether the page should be indexed
After duplicates are dropped, index selection is the decision to keep the page or not

stages.title: Pages Written for People
stages.description: The page should be useful to a person who arrived on purpose. There is no secret word count, and repeating keywords is against the spam rules.
learningObjectives: Describe people-first content in Google's own questions
Name signs that a page was written mainly to rank
State that E-E-A-T is not itself a ranking factor
Drop the ideas Google says not to chase

explainBack.question: You are about to publish a page aimed at a search phrase. Explain how you would tell whether it is people-first, and which common SEO habits Google says not to bother with.
rubric: People-first content is written for an audience that would find it useful if they came to the site directly
Warning signs include writing mainly to attract search visits, covering many topics without expertise, summarizing others without adding value, and chasing a supposed preferred word count
Using automation, including AI, mainly to manipulate rankings violates the spam policies
Google Search does not use the keywords meta tag, keyword stuffing is against the spam policies, and content length alone is not a ranking target
E-E-A-T is not a specific ranking factor; trust matters most, and raters do not directly set ranks

resources.title: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
resources.description: Google's questions for judging whether a page was made for people or for rankings.
keyPoints: Ranking systems are meant to prioritize helpful, reliable information created for people, not content created to manipulate rankings
People-first content has an audience that would find it useful if they came directly, and it shows first-hand knowledge
Search-engine-first warning signs include mass topics, heavy automation, summarizing others without added value, and writing to a rumored word count
SEO is useful when it helps search engines understand people-first content
E-E-A-T is not itself a ranking factor; trust is the most important of those aspects, and search raters do not directly control how pages rank

resources.title: SEO Starter Guide: The Basics
resources.description: Google's starter guide: useful pages, honest titles, and the tactics it says to ignore.
keyPoints: SEO helps search engines understand content and helps people decide whether to visit; there is no secret that automatically ranks a site first
Useful content is readable, original, current, and helpful; readers may search with different words for the same thing, and Google can match related queries
Changes can take hours or months; a few weeks is a reasonable wait before judging a change
Google Search does not use the keywords meta tag, keyword stuffing violates the spam policies, and there is no magical minimum or maximum word count
Keywords in the domain or URL path barely affect ranking beyond breadcrumbs, and E-E-A-T is not a ranking factor

stages.title: Titles and Snippets
stages.description: The title link and the snippet are what a person sees before they click. Google may rewrite either one from the page itself.
learningObjectives: Write a title that is unique to the page
Explain where Google gets a title link
Explain where a snippet comes from
Write a meta description that is specific to one URL

explainBack.question: Your page's title in search results is not the title you wrote, and the snippet is a sentence from the middle of the page. Explain why that can happen, and how you would write the title and the description anyway.
rubric: A title link is the headline of a search result; Google generates it automatically from the title element, the visible heading, other prominent text, and links that point at the page
A good title is unique, clear, concise, and accurate; vague titles, keyword stuffing, and the same boilerplate on every page are the problems Google calls out
Google may replace a title that is half-empty, obsolete, inaccurate, or in a different language from the page
Snippets are created from the page content and can differ by query; the meta description is used when it describes the page better
Each important URL should have its own description; a long string of keywords is less likely to be shown

resources.title: Influencing your title links in search results
resources.description: How Google builds the clickable title, and the title-writing habits that make it rewrite yours.
keyPoints: A title link is the title of a search result; Google determines it automatically, and you can only indicate a preference
Every page should have a title element that is descriptive and concise; the title link is truncated to fit the device
Avoid keyword stuffing, the same boilerplate on every page, and a site slogan repeated on every URL
Google looks at the title element, the main visual title, headings, og:title, other prominent text, and anchor text pointing at the page
Google may rewrite a title that is half-empty, out of date, inaccurate, or written in a different script from the page

resources.title: Control your snippets in search results
resources.description: Where the description under a result comes from, and how to write a meta description Google might use.
keyPoints: A snippet is the description under a result; Google creates it from page content and may show different snippets for different searches
The meta description is used when it gives a more accurate description than text taken from the page
nosnippet can prevent a snippet, and max-snippet can suggest a maximum length
Write a unique description for each page; identical descriptions across a site are not helpful
A meta description that is a long string of keywords is less likely to be displayed as the snippet

stages.title: Links People and Google Can Follow
stages.description: A link Google can crawl is an ordinary anchor with an href. The words in that link should say where it goes.
learningObjectives: Name the HTML Google can reliably crawl as a link
Write anchor text that makes sense on its own
Give every important page a link from somewhere else on the site
Use nofollow, sponsored, or ugc for the cases Google names

explainBack.question: A button on your site looks like a link, but it is a span with a click handler, and the visible words are 'click here.' Explain why that is a weak link for Google, and how you would write the link instead.
rubric: Google generally crawls a link only when it is an a element with an href that resolves to a real URL
Spans, router attributes, and anchors that only have an onclick are not the recommended pattern
Anchor text should be descriptive, concise, and meaningful if you read it alone; 'click here' is too generic
Keyword stuffing in anchor text violates the spam policies, and there is no ideal number of links on a page

Every page you care about should be linked from at least one other page on the site; use nofollow when you do not trust the target, sponsored when you were paid, and ugc or nofollow on links visitors insert

resources.title: Link best practices for Google
resources.description: Which links Google can extract, and how to write the text of those links.
keyPoints: Google uses links both as a relevancy signal and to discover new pages
A crawlable link is generally an a element with an href; Google cannot reliably extract URLs from tags that only act like links because of script
javascript: hrefs are not recommended; a normal path or absolute URL is
Good anchor text is descriptive and concise; generic text such as 'click here' fails if you read the link alone
Every page you care about should have a link from at least one other page; use nofollow for untrusted targets, sponsored for paid links, and ugc or nofollow for links users insert

stages.title: See Whether Google Found the Page
stages.description: Search Console shows crawl, index, and the queries that brought people. The URL Inspection tool is the place to look at one address.
learningObjectives: Say what Search Console is for and how often to open it
Name the first reports to check
Use URL Inspection for one address
State what the live test does not prove

explainBack.question: A page you published last week is not in the results. Explain which tool you would open, what it can tell you about that one URL, and what a live test still does not prove.
rubric: Search Console reports how Google crawls, indexes, and serves a site you have verified; you do not need to sign in every day
A sitemap can speed discovery but is not required; the performance report shows queries, pages, impressions, and clicks
URL Inspection shows Google's indexed version of one URL in the property, and it can test the live URL and request crawling
The indexed data is where you see the Google-selected canonical; the live test cannot predict the canonical
The test does not check quality guidelines, manual actions, security issues, or legal removals, and a live test does not say whether a video is indexed

resources.title: Get started with Search Console
resources.description: What to do first in Search Console, and which reports answer which questions.
keyPoints: Search Console shows how Google crawls, indexes, and serves a site, and what you can do to improve how it appears
You do not need to sign in every day; Google emails when it finds new issues, and a monthly look is enough for a stable site
Start by verifying ownership, then review index coverage, and consider submitting a sitemap even though discovery does not require one
The performance report breaks traffic down by query, page, and country, with impressions and clicks
The URL Inspection tool shows the index status of one page, can test a live URL, and can request a crawl

resources.title: URL Inspection tool
resources.description: How to inspect one URL, what the indexed report shows, and what the test skips.
keyPoints: The tool reports Google's indexed version of a URL in the current property and can test whether that URL might be indexable
You can see why a URL could or could not be indexed, inspect the live page, request indexing, and view a rendered screenshot
The Google-selected canonical is available on the indexed version only; the live test cannot predict it
The URL you inspect must belong to the property you have open
Results do not test quality or security guidelines, manual actions, legal removals, or whether a video is indexed; a live test only says whether a video was detected

resources.title: URL Inspection Tool - Google Search Console Training
resources.description: A Search Console training video on inspecting one URL, testing it live, and asking for a crawl.
keyPoints: The tool shows Google's indexed version and a live test of one page
Paste the full URL into the inspection box; the URL has to be in the property you have open
After the report loads you can test the live URL, ask Google to crawl the page, and view the crawled page
The tool is for web pages and reports web search

stages.title: Whether the Page Is Pleasant to Use
stages.description: Page experience is several things at once. Core Web Vitals are used in ranking. A perfect score does not put a page first.
learningObjectives: List the questions Google uses for page experience
Name LCP, INP, and CLS and the thresholds Google gives
Explain that there is no single page-experience ranking signal
Keep relevance ahead of a perfect vitals score

explainBack.question: Your Core Web Vitals report is 'good,' and a slower competitor still outranks you. Explain what those metrics measure, and what they do not guarantee.
rubric: Page experience includes Core Web Vitals, HTTPS, mobile display, ads that do not bury the content, and no intrusive interstitials
There is no single page-experience ranking signal
LCP should be within 2.5 seconds, INP under 200 milliseconds, and CLS under 0.1
Core Web Vitals are used by ranking systems, but a good score does not guarantee a top rank
Search still tries to show the most relevant content even when page experience is poor; experience matters more when many helpful pages exist

resources.title: Understanding page experience in Google Search results
resources.description: Google's list of page-experience questions, and how much they matter next to relevance.
keyPoints: Core ranking systems reward a good page experience across many aspects, not one or two tricks
The self-check covers Core Web Vitals, HTTPS, mobile display, ads that do not block the content, and avoiding intrusive interstitials
There is no single page-experience signal
Core Web Vitals are used in ranking; other page-experience aspects do not directly raise rank, though they make the page more satisfying
Search still seeks the most relevant content even if page experience is poor; experience contributes when lots of helpful content exists for the query

resources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results
resources.description: The three Core Web Vitals metrics and the numbers Google calls a good experience.
keyPoints: Core Web Vitals measure real-world loading, interactivity, and visual stability
Largest Contentful Paint should occur within 2.5 seconds of the page starting to load
Interaction to Next Paint should be under 200 milliseconds
Cumulative Layout Shift should be under 0.1
Search Console's Core Web Vitals report shows how pages perform; a good score supports Search and is not the whole of ranking

stages.title: What Google Calls Spam
stages.description: Spam is an attempt to deceive people or to push a page up. Buying links, hiding text, and generating piles of empty pages are named policies.
learningObjectives: Define spam in Google's terms
Recognize cloaking, hidden text, and keyword stuffing
Qualify a paid link so it does not pass ranking credit
Explain scaled content abuse, including empty AI pages

explainBack.question: Someone offers to sell you links, and someone else offers to generate hundreds of AI pages aimed at search. Explain which policies those offers run into, and what would make a paid link allowed.
rubric: Spam means techniques that deceive users or manipulate Search into featuring content, including attempts to manipulate generative AI responses
Sites that violate the policies may rank lower or not appear; detection can be automated or a manual action
Cloaking shows different content to users and to search engines in order to manipulate rankings; keyword stuffing and hidden text or links are separate policies
Buying or selling links for ranking is link spam; a paid link is allowed when it uses rel=nofollow or rel=sponsored
Scaled content abuse is many pages made mainly to manipulate rankings, including generative AI pages that add little or no value for users

resources.title: Spam policies for Google web search
resources.description: The practices that can remove a page from results or push it down.
keyPoints: Spam is techniques used to deceive users or to manipulate Search, including attempts to manipulate generative AI responses in Search
Violations can lead to a lower rank or removal, through automated systems or a manual action
Cloaking shows search engines different content from users; hidden text, keyword stuffing, and doorway pages are separate named practices
Buying or selling links to affect ranking is link spam; paid links are allowed when marked nofollow or sponsored
Scaled content abuse includes using generative AI to produce many pages that provide little or no value, however the pages were made

stages.title: Structured Data and Rich Results
stages.description: Structured data is a label for what is already on the page. It can make a result eligible for a rich result. It does not promise one.
learningObjectives: Say what structured data is for
Prefer JSON-LD when you can maintain it
Keep the markup about content the visitor can see
Test the markup and then watch Search Console

explainBack.question: You add recipe markup to a page that does not show a recipe, hoping for stars in search. Explain what structured data is allowed to describe, which format Google recommends, and what a valid markup still does not guarantee.
rubric: Structured data is a standard way to classify the content of a page, such as the ingredients and time on a recipe
It can make a page eligible for a rich result; eligibility is not a promise that the feature will show
Do not put markup on an empty page, and do not mark up information the user cannot see
Google recommends JSON-LD when it is easiest to maintain; Microdata and RDFa are also supported when valid
Required properties must be present and accurate; test with the Rich Results Test, then watch the rich result reports after the page is deployed

resources.title: Introduction to structured data markup in Google Search
resources.description: What markup does for a result, which formats Google reads, and how to tell whether it helped.
keyPoints: Structured data gives Google explicit clues about a page, such as ingredients, time, and calories on a recipe
Valid markup can make a page eligible for rich results; it does not by itself guarantee that feature
The markup must describe content on that page that a visitor can see; do not create empty pages just to hold it
Google recommends JSON-LD; Microdata and RDFa are equally acceptable when the markup is valid
Include every required property, prefer fewer accurate fields over a pile of incomplete ones, and check the Rich Results Test before you rely on the page

name: SEO
description: Learn how Google finds a page and what you can honestly change: crawl and index, people-first writing, titles and snippets, links, Search Console, page experience, spam rules, and structured data.
